conversation_history.content: hey! I'm Jordan, senior in info sciences with a music minor. I graduate in May and I want to try something new before I leave. I've been thinking about improv comedy, and maybe something UX/design-related since that's what I want to do after college.

Not yet, still figuring it out. Side question: I want to get better at Figma before applying to UX jobs. Where should I start? I've only used it for basic wireframes.

If you're already making wireframes, the next steps are the features hiring managers expect to see in a portfolio. First, learn auto layout well. It lets frames resize like real interfaces and it's the biggest difference between beginner and intermediate files. Second, build reusable components with variants, for example a button with default, hover, and disabled states, and use them across screens. Third, set up text and color styles so the design is consistent. Fourth, prototype a full flow, like signing up or checking out, with interactions between screens. Figma's own learning resources and community files are free and good for this. A practical exercise is to redesign one flow from an app you use every day. Document the problem, your sketches, the iterations, and the final prototype, because portfolios are judged on process as much as polish. Once that feels comfortable, a small design system with tokens, a component library, and one documented pattern is a strong portfolio piece.

ok that's a good plan. Anyway, nothing else schedule-wise right now. Random question though: for IS 445, what's the actual difference between a bar chart and a histogram? My TA marked me down for using the wrong one.

Good question. They look similar but encode different things. A bar chart compares values across separate categories, like the number of students per major. The bars are usually separated by gaps and the order of categories is arbitrary or chosen for readability. A histogram shows the distribution of one continuous numeric variable, like commute times, by splitting it into adjacent bins and counting how many observations fall into each. The bars touch because the bins are contiguous, and the x-axis is a numeric scale with a fixed order. Rule of thumb: if your x-axis is labels, use a bar chart. If it's ranges of a number, use a histogram and pick the bin width carefully, because different widths can change the visible shape of the distribution.

Could you help me tighten a resume bullet? Right now it says 'Worked on a team that made a dashboard for the library to see how many people use study rooms.'

Can you help me think about how to structure my capstone presentation? It's 15 minutes plus Q&A, and our project is a redesign of a local nonprofit's volunteer sign-up site.

For a 15-minute capstone talk about a redesign, a problem-to-impact structure works well. Spend about 2 minutes on context: who the nonprofit is, who signs up to volunteer, and why it matters. Spend 3 minutes on the problem, showing evidence such as drop-off points in the old flow, quotes from user interviews, or usability test results. Spend 2 minutes on your process: research methods, personas or journey maps, and how many rounds of iteration you did. The redesign should be the centerpiece at about 5 minutes. Walk through the new flow as a story about one volunteer, and show a before and after for the most important screens. Use about 2 minutes for results and impact, such as task completion time, error rates, or stakeholder feedback, and be honest about limitations. Close in 1 minute with what you'd do next. For Q&A, prepare backup slides on accessibility, technical constraints, and why you rejected alternative designs, because those questions come up often. Rehearse with a timer at least twice.

Unrelated, but is it worth buying a really heavy winter coat or can I get away with layers? This is my last winter here lol

Champaign winters often have stretches well below freezing, and wind across the open quads makes it feel colder, especially at bus stops. Since you rely on the bus, a warm, windproof coat is probably worth it, ideally one that covers your hips. Pair it with a hat, gloves, and warm socks. If you'd rather not buy something expensive for one winter, a mid-weight insulated jacket with a fleece layer underneath and a windproof shell works well too. Thrift stores and end-of-season sales are good places to look.
Do you have tips for practicing viola more efficiently? I only get maybe 30-40 minutes a day between everything.

With 30-40 minutes, structure matters more than total time. Try this split. Spend 5 minutes warming up with slow scales and long tones, focusing on tone and bow distribution instead of speed. Spend 10 minutes on technique targeted at whatever your current repertoire needs, like shifting, string crossings, or a specific bowing pattern. Spend 15-20 minutes on repertoire, but don't play pieces top to bottom. Pick the 2-3 hardest passages and loop them slowly with a metronome, raising the tempo only when you can play a passage cleanly three times in a row. Use the last few minutes to play through a longer section for continuity. Record yourself once or twice a week, because it's the fastest way to hear intonation and rhythm problems you miss while playing. On rehearsal days, focus your short practice on the orchestra passages the conductor flagged. If you can split practice into two short sessions, that often helps retention more than one longer block.

Random stats question for my other class: what is a p-value actually? I keep seeing 'probability the null is true' and my professor says that's wrong.

Your professor is right. A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It's computed under the null, so it can't be the probability that the null is true. A small p-value means your data would be surprising if the null were true, which counts as evidence against it. It doesn't tell you how big or important an effect is, and 0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature. Pair p-values with effect sizes and confidence intervals.
One more for IS 467: what's the difference between a LEFT JOIN and an INNER JOIN? I always mix them up.

An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. If you join students to enrollments, students with no enrollments disappear from the result. A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, the one written first, plus matching rows from the right table. Where there's no match, the right-side columns are NULL, so students with no enrollments still appear with empty enrollment fields. A quick way to remember: a LEFT JOIN never loses rows from the left table. A common use is finding missing data. LEFT JOIN, then filter WHERE right_table.id IS NULL to get students with no enrollments. Be careful putting conditions on the right table in the WHERE clause after a LEFT JOIN, because that can quietly turn it back into an inner join. Put those conditions in the ON clause instead.
